source.title: GRASP: A Rehearsal Policy for Efficient Online Continual Learning
source.venue: 3rd Conference on Lifelong Learning Agents, PMLR 274, 2025

assessments.primary_source_quality: High. Peer-reviewed PMLR paper with a directly specified prototypical-first/easy-to-hard sampling policy, comparison against 17 rehearsal policies, large-scale ImageNet continual-learning experiments, five text-classification datasets, and compute/memory-overhead analysis. No independent replication was located in this pass.
assessments.quantitative_result: The primary PMLR abstract reports that GRASP achieves higher continual-learning accuracy than 17 comparison rehearsal policies on ImageNet and reaches the same performance as uniform class-balanced replay with 40% fewer model updates. It also reports effectiveness across five text-classification datasets while adding little compute or memory overhead over uniform selection.
assessments.matched_baseline: Strong for the native mechanism: GRASP is explicitly compared with uniform class-balanced rehearsal and a broad set of 17 other selection policies in the same continual-learning setup. The 40% fewer-updates result directly targets efficiency at matched performance.
assessments.ablation_or_causal_support: Moderately strong to strong for the proposed rehearsal-order/selection policy in online continual learning. The exact roles of prototypicality definition, curriculum schedule and buffer composition are coupled within GRASP, but the policy is a concrete intervention rather than an inferred remedy.
assessments.reproducibility_or_artifacts: Peer-reviewed PMLR paper with explicit method/evaluation. This comparator did not independently run code and did not establish an independent reproduction.
assessments.failure_evidence: The study also implies that uniform replay is not always sample-efficient; however, it does not establish that easy-to-hard scheduling is optimal in arbitrary memory/query domains.
scope_limits: Online continual parameter learning with replay buffers, primarily ImageNet plus text classification, not autonomous-agent episodic memory retrieval.
Prototypicality/easiness is defined in supervised representation/class settings and may be difficult to map to heterogeneous research evidence.
The 40% update reduction is a native continual-learning efficiency result, not a token/tool-call reduction for LLM agents.

original_method_vs_o_adaptation.original_method_evidence: B+ for GRASP's easy-to-hard rehearsal selection as a direct continual-learning mechanism under the reported supervised replay settings.
original_method_vs_o_adaptation.o_specific_adaptation: C for using analogous prototypical-first/harder-later context or research-memory routing in O until a matched retrieval-order experiment demonstrates downstream benefit at fixed memory, calls and evidence coverage.

source.title: Replay can provably increase forgetting
source.venue: 4th Conference on Lifelong Learning Agents, PMLR 330, 2026

assessments.primary_source_quality: Very strong for the scoped failure claim. The peer-reviewed work provides formal analysis in over-parameterized continual linear regression, constructs worst-case harmful-replay tasks, proves distributional settings where random replay increases forgetting in expectation, demonstrates similar behavior with neural networks trained by SGD, and adds a standard-benchmark empirical study.
assessments.quantitative_result: The key evidence is structural rather than one headline effect size: even in noiseless settings where sufficiently informative replay could eliminate forgetting, forgetting is non-monotonic in the number/choice of replay samples; there are worst-case task constructions where replay is harmful and distributions where random replay increases forgetting in expectation. Neural-network and standard-benchmark experiments show the phenomenon is not confined to the linear proof setting.
assessments.matched_baseline: Strong for the failure proposition because replay amount/sample choice and task-subspace relationships are explicitly varied against lower/no replay conditions under the model analyzed. The paper is not an experiment on LLM context retrieval or external-memory prompting.
assessments.ablation_or_causal_support: Strong for the causal/scoped claim that more/random replay can increase forgetting depending on task/sample geometry. It does not identify a universal compatibility selector that prevents harmful replay in arbitrary settings.
assessments.reproducibility_or_artifacts: Peer-reviewed PMLR publication with formal proofs and empirical sections; no independent reproduction was run by this comparator.
assessments.external_replication: Not required for the mathematical construction itself; independent empirical replication of the neural/benchmark phenomenon was not identified in this pass.
assessments.failure_evidence: Direct and unusually strong negative evidence against the monotonic assumption that adding more replay samples is necessarily safer for retention.
scope_limits: Formal results are for continual linear-regression task-subspace settings; neural experiments broaden but do not universalize the claim.
The result does not say replay is generally harmful; it says benefit depends on sample choice and task relationship and can be non-monotonic.
Transferring the lesson from parameter-replay geometry to prompt/context memory is an analogy requiring direct testing.
It offers a guardrail/falsification target rather than a complete replay-selection algorithm.

original_method_vs_o_adaptation.original_method_evidence: A- for the scoped failure claim that replay can provably and empirically increase forgetting under specific task/sample relationships.
original_method_vs_o_adaptation.o_specific_adaptation: C+/B- only for the broader design rule 'do not assume more context/replay is safer' in O; direct O context-interference or memory-selection evidence is needed before treating parameter-replay geometry as O-specific mechanism evidence.

cross_source_synthesis: These two peer-reviewed sources are complementary rather than contradictory: GRASP demonstrates that structured replay selection/order can improve efficiency, while the 2026 theory/empirical work proves that indiscriminate replay quantity is not monotonic and can be harmful.

The strongest transferable principle is not 'easy memories first' or 'less replay'; it is that replay policy is an intervention whose sample compatibility, order and update cost must be measured rather than treating memory membership/volume as sufficient.
Any O analogy should be tested directly because supervised parameter rehearsal and prompt/context retrieval have different interference mechanisms.
